How to get Apple TV

You can subscribe to Apple TV on Apple’s website here, or via the Apple TV app on your device. It costs $12.99/£9.99 a month, which you can cancel at any time (Read: How to cancel an Apple subscription). You can also opt for a one-year subscription for $99/£89, which essentially gives you two months free each year.

Apple also offers various trials so that you can try out Apple TV before you subscribe. Take a look at our article explaining all the ways you can watch Apple TV for free, and the best Apple TV deals you can get.

Students can get Apple TV for free with an already subsidized Apple Music subscription.

Best shows on Apple TV

There’s far too much content on Apple TV to sift through it all yourself. If you’re looking for something to watch and don’t know where to start, here are a few of the Macworld staff’s favorite shows, series, and movies.

Bad Sisters

  • Synopsis: A dark comedy about a group of Irish sisters who find themselves at the center of a life insurance investigation after John Paul–the abusive husband to one of the sisters–dies unexpectedly.
  • Number of seasons: 2
  • Release date: August 19, 2022

Black Bird

  • Synopsis: A gripping miniseries about a convicted con artist who works for the FBI to try to get a serial killer’s confession before he is released from prison. Based on the true story of James Keene and Larry Hall.
  • Number of seasons: 1
  • Release date: July 8, 2022

Pluribus

  • Synopsis: A mysterious virus-like pathogen turns the entire human race into a peaceful hive-mind, except for a handful of individuals. Created by Vince Gilligan, of Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul fame.
  • Number of seasons: 1
  • Release date: November 17, 2025

Severance

  • Synopsis: A combination of dystopian sci-fi drama and workplace comedy about a company where employees are “severed”–when at work, they can’t remember their outside lives, and vice-versa.
  • Number of seasons: 2
  • Release date: February 18, 2022

Shrinking

  • Synopsis: A surprisingly quick-witted comedy about a therapist who has trouble dealing with the death of his wife and his eccentric patients.
  • Number of seasons: 3
  • Release date: January 27, 2023

Slow Horses

  • Synopsis: Gary Oldman turns in a great performance as the cranky leader of a band of misfit spies.
  • Number of seasons: 6
  • Release date: April 1, 2022

Ted Lasso

  • Synopsis: Apple’s fish-out-of-water comedy/drama about a midwestern college football coach who heads to England to coach Premier League soccer is a breakout hit for good reason.
  • Number of seasons: 4
  • Release date: August 14, 2020

The Morning Show

  • Synopsis: Big star power and a fantastic performance by Jenniffer Aniston highlight this fast-paced drama that goes behind the scenes of a fictional morning news program.
  • Number of seasons: 4
  • Release date: November 1, 2019

Full list of Apple TV shows and series

These are all the episodic series you can currently watch on Apple TV, including both recurring and limited series. This list is in alphabetical order.

Full list of Apple TV movies and short films

If you have an old “cheese-grater” Mac Pro, you probably don’t want to part with it. You look at it and wonder what you’re going to do with it, since it can’t be upgraded. Seems like a waste to throw it out, and you won’t get nearly enough to make it worth selling. Well, a Canadian mechatronics enthusiast understands your predicament and has set out to do something about it.

Stefan Bond has launched the Mac Pro 7,1 (A1991) ATX Conversion Kit project on Kickstarter. The kit can be used to install “modern PC hardware” into the chassis of a Mac Pro–specifically, the Mac Pro that was introduced in 2019 and identified with the model number 7,1. Since it was built with Mac hardware in mind, you can’t simply gut it and pop in a PC motherboard, a gigantic graphics card, and other components. The Conversion Kit will allow you to do that by providing a main motherboard and PSU mounting plate, hard drive sled assemblies and cables, Mac Pro fan-adapter PCBs, and more.

To be clear, this is a kit that enables you to install PC components (which aren’t included) for building a PC that runs Windows. There’s no official way to upgrade the Mac Pro with Apple components. If you really want to run macOS, you should be able to turn this into a Hackintosh after building it.

Bond has a goal of $10,000 for his Kickstarter, and a bid of $699 in Canadian currency (about $500 in the U.S.) gets you a full conversion kit. If you don’t have a Mac Pro but just want to contribute to the spirit of the project, you can chip in CA$10, and your name will be mentioned in the final project video.

Apple discontinued the Mac Pro earlier this year, ending a 20-year run for the Mac Pro brand. The latest time it was updated was in 2023, when Apple released it with an M2 Ultra chip. When this design was introduced in 2019, it had Intel processors. Apple offers the Mac Studio as its top Mac workstation, but it doesn’t have anywhere near the character of its old metal towers.

Apple has finally brought a touch interface to the Mac, 43 years after the first commercial PC with a touchscreen, the HP 150. It’s a momentous event in Apple history, one that longtime Mac users never thought would come.

The new laptop is going to be mainly referred to as the “touchscreen MacBook Pro,” and there’s a lot of talk about the feature. But if you think of the new laptop only in terms of Touch, you’re missing the point. There’s a reason why Apple calls it the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It’s clumsy and lengthy, but notice how “Touch” isn’t one of the words.

“Touch” isn’t in the name because it’s not the most important new feature of the new MacBook Pro. In fact, Apple has a link to a white paper about the PROLED Display on the product wesbite, and Touch isn’t mentioned at all. I think it’s the least important feature, and there are other aspects of the laptop that are more important and have implications for other MacBooks down the line.

OLED takes the lead

The display is the most important feature, but not because of touch, but because it’s a tandem OLED display that can “deliver the kind of visual fidelity pros have been dreaming of,” according to Apple. Considering Apple’s long history of producing the best quality laptop displays, I’m inclined to believe that statement.

Apple

Look at these specs. This is on a laptop? Damn.

  • 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio
  • XDR brightness: Up to 1000 nits sustained full-screen; 2000 nits peak (HDR content only)
  • SDR brightness: Up to 1000 nits sustained full-screen; 2000 nits peak (outdoor)
  • ProMotion adaptive refresh rates
  • 1.00 percent reflectance, lower than traditional OLED displays
  • P3 + Adobe RGB wide color gamuts
  • Apple Color-Matching Functions 2026
  • Medical imaging support

That’s easily one of the best, if not the best display ever put in a laptop. Can a display on a laptop be so good-looking that you’ll never want to take your eyes off it? If it can, count on Apple to make it.

What’s even more exciting is what it means for the rest of the MacBook lineup in the future. Several reports have said OLED is coming to the MacBook Air, possibly in 2028, and though it probably won’t be on the same level as the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display—consider the difference between the iPad mini and the iPad Pro—it’ll still be a major upgrade from the current LED-backlit IPS panel.

Lighter design

A few days ago, I was in the office with my 16-inch MacBook Pro in my backpack. I put my backpack on my desk, and it landed with a loud thud. My co-worker (a PC fanboy) was shocked. “What’s with the rocks in your bag?” he exclaimed

The new MacBook Pro is nearly a pound lighter. That might not sound like much, but it makes a difference if you’re moving around often, or if you’re like me and you have an hour-long commute on public transportation. Hopefully, that thud won’t be as resonant with the new laptop.

It’ll be interesting to see if the advances Apple made to achieve the smaller and lighter MacBook Pro will carry over to the other MacBooks. Imagine if the MacBook Neo and the 13-inch MacBook Air, Apple’s lightest laptops at 2.7 pounds, were closer to 2 pounds.

Dynamic Island

The notch on the MacBooks is there because the bezel is too thin to fit the FaceTime camera, but it’s also just sort of… there. It’s not really obtrusive, because it sits above the usable screen space in the status bar, but it still feels like a vestigial part of the laptop with no real purpose.

Apple

The Dynamic Island replaces the notch, and it’s now a functional anchor of the Mac. It works as it does on the iPhone, so you know it’ll be a useful home for Spotlight search and Lite Activities. I’ve come to appreciate how it’s used on the iPhone, so I’m excited to see it become a natural extension of macOS.

Will the Dynamic Island make it to other MacBooks? It would be a shame if Apple decided it was a premium feature for only the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, but I can see that happening. Apple won’t switch from the notch to the Dynamic Island until the other MacBooks upgrade their display tech, so we won’t know for some time.

Glowing Apple logo

It’s just a logo, but as Mac users and Apple fans, that Apple logo has meaning. When the glowing Apple was introduced in the 1999 PowerBook G3, it made a statement (even though it was upside down for the first couple of years). It told people we were proud Mac users. We mourned the loss of the logo in 2015.

But the glowing logo and the statement it brings are back. But this time it comes as a flex, the way that Cosmic Orange was for the iPhone 17 Pro. People who know Macs will see it and know you’ve got the new MacBook Pro. As for the people who don’t know Macs, well, they’ll see it and be envious. Best of all, the glowing Apple icon won’t be upside down when the lid is open. And now that it’s a little screen of its own, you can even turn it off if you want.

Apple

What is it? The 13-inch MacBook Air is Apple’s thin and light laptop for everyday use, offering more performance and features than the cheaper MacBook Neo.

What’s new? Apple introduced the M5 MacBook Air in March 2026, featuring the M5 chip with its faster CPU and GPU. The base configuration now starts with 512GB of storage (double the previous model), along with faster SSD speeds, more memory bandwidth, and support for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.

Who’s it for? It’s perfect for students and everyday users who want a lightweight laptop that’s easy to carry, and powerful enough for working, studying, browsing, and doing light creative work. If you want a larger screen there is a 15-inch MacBook Air, which we discuss below.

How much does the 13-inch MacBook Air cost? The entry-level 13-inch M5 MacBook Air costs from $1,299/£1,299, that’s up $200/£200 from the launch price of $1,099/£1,099. You can create build-to-order models with more memory (up to 32GB) or storage (up to 4TB).

What are the specifications? The standard specs for the M5 MacBook Air offer an improvement compared to the previous generation. The MacBook Air now ships with 512GB SSD as standard.

  • Apple M5, 10-core CPU, 8-core GPU, 16GB memory, 512GB SSD, two Thunderbolt 4 ports: $1,299/£1,299.
  • Apple M5, 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB memory, 512GB SSD, two Thunderbolt 4 ports: $1,399/£1,399.
  • Additional options: Up to 32GB memory, 4TB storage.

What are display specifications?

  • While referred to as 13-inch, when measured diagonally the screen is 13.6-inches.
  • The 13.6-inch Liquid Retina on the M5 MacBook Air display has a native resolution of 2,560×1,664 and 500 nits brightness.
  • The MacBook Air M5 can support two external displays.

How do I connect stuff? The M5 MacBook Air models supports Thunderbolt 4, which means that they can support a dual monitor set up. If you want to connect USB-A devices, you need either a USB-C to USB-A adapter, like Apple’s $19 / £19 one, or a USB-C hub that has USB-A ports. In the U.K. and Europe Apple has stopped including a Power Adapter in the box, so you will need to buy one separately. See our round-up of the best USB-C hubs and adapters.

The 2026 MacBook Air offers Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) for connecting to a network. It also provides built-in Bluetooth (6) for wirelessly connecting a mouse or other peripherals. If you want to connect to an ethernet network, you need an adapter.

How fast is it? In our tests the M5 saw consistent gains over the M4 in the previous generation, as you can see in our Mac processor benchmarks. In some benchmarks the M5 even beats the M1 Ultra. If you are upgrading from an old Mac – especially if it is one with an Intel chip – you will see a huge difference.

Any other considerations? The MacBook Air is more than fast enough for everyday use and occasional creative work. Its fanless design keeps it silent, but performance can drop during sustained demanding tasks as it reduces speed to control heat. If you regularly run lengthy video exports, large code builds or other intensive workloads, a MacBook Pro with active cooling is a better choice. Memory and internal storage cannot be upgraded after purchase, so choose a configuration that meets your likely longer-term needs. Prioritize enough memory for your apps; you can add storage later with an external SSD. The Air still uses M5, while Apple now offers M6 versions of the standard MacBook Pro, iMac and Mac mini. An M6 MacBook Air could follow in spring 2027. If you need a new laptop now, the M5 Air remains a capable option, particularly at a discount.

Why we recommend the 13-inch MacBook Air: The MacBook Air is a great choice for someone who does general-purpose work and moves around a lot, such as a student or a self-employed person.

What’s best, MacBook Air or MacBook Pro?

We explore this question in detail in our MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro comparison. The MacBook Air is the best choice for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work, studying and many creative tasks. The MacBook Pro is worth considering if you need sustained performance for demanding workloads, more ports or a more advanced display.

The entry-level MacBook Air costs $1,299/£1,299, although you can often spend less by shopping around – we regularly round up the best MacBook Air deals. If you want more screen space without paying for professional-level performance, the 15-inch MacBook Air is considerably cheaper than a 14-inch MacBook Pro.

Within the MacBook Pro range, the standard 14-inch M6 model provides a middle ground between the Air and the more expensive M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations. Its fan helps maintain performance during longer processing tasks, while its Liquid Retina XDR display, HDMI port and SDXC card slot add flexibility.

The M5 Pro and M5 Max models suit more demanding professional workloads, offering more CPU and GPU cores, higher memory capacities and Thunderbolt 5. M5 Pro is a strong option for software development, photography and video editing. Consider M5 Max if your work benefits from its additional graphics power, media engines or higher memory ceiling; spending more won’t necessarily make everyday tasks noticeably faster.

You can also choose a MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR touchscreen. Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, these models add an OLED display, touch controls alongside the keyboard and trackpad, Dynamic Island, and a thinner, lighter design. Starting at $2,899/£2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399/£3,399 for the 16-inch, they cost $400/£400 more than equivalent non-touch M5 Pro models. They use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip families, so the main reasons to pay extra are the display, portability and touch input.

Choosing between a 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro comes down to workspace, portability, battery life and price. The larger model gives you more room for editing timelines, coding and multitasking, while the 14-inch is easier to carry. Both sizes offer powerful Pro and Max configurations. For external monitors, current M5 Pro models support up to three displays and M5 Max models support up to four, depending on resolution and refresh rate.

For a tighter budget, the MacBook Neo lowers the starting price of a Mac laptop to $699/£699. It’s worth comparing its compromises with a discounted previous-generation MacBook Air before deciding.

2.

Should I upgrade from my Intel Mac?

Yes. It’s time! We are now more than six years into Apple’s transition from Intel processors to its own silicon that includes CPU, GPU, and unified memory. The transition began with the introduction of the M1 in November 2020. Since June 2023 every Mac Apple sells uses Apple’s own chips rather than Intel processors.

If you’ve yet to upgrade your Intel Mac to one powered by Apple’s silicon what are you waiting for? If you are concerned that a must-have app doesn’t run on an M-series Mac, consider finding a new app because the performance gains are tremendous.

Another good reason to replace an Intel Mac is that Apple’s support for these models is winding down. macOS Golden Gate, released in September 2026, is the first major version of macOS to support no Intel Macs. Intel Macs compatible with older versions of macOS may continue receiving security updates for a limited period, but they are now outside Apple’s current feature-release cycle. Apple does not guarantee how long those updates will continue, and machines limited to macOS Sequoia are likely to lose support sooner than those capable of running macOS Tahoe. 4.

What specs do I really need for my Mac?

Chip: The specs you need depend on what you plan to do with your Mac. For web browsing, email, office apps and light photo editing, a standard M-series chip is more than sufficient. The M6 is available in the Mac mini, iMac and standard 14-inch MacBook Pro, while the MacBook Air uses M5. The budget MacBook Neo uses an A18 Pro chip. A newer generation number doesn’t automatically make a chip better for every workload: compare its CPU, GPU, memory and capabilities with what your apps actually need.

If you regularly work with complex spreadsheets, large Photoshop files, audio projects, video editing or more demanding games, look at a Pro chip. The M5 Pro Mac mini, for example, offers up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU and up to 64GB unified memory.

A Max chip is worth considering for demanding graphics, complex 3D work, high-resolution video production or projects that need more memory than a Pro configuration supports. Many developers, photographers and video editors will be well served by a Pro chip. The M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and up to 128GB unified memory, depending on configuration.

For professional video production, 3D work, software development and other intensive workloads, a Max chip is more appropriate. The Mac Studio with M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and as much as 128GB unified memory. 

The M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU and 512GB unified memory, is aimed at the most extreme workloads, including VFX, scientific computing and running very large AI models locally.

GPU: One of the biggest differences between Apple’s chips is GPU performance. Standard M-series chips are easily sufficient for everyday graphics, casual gaming and light creative work. Pro chips add considerably more GPU power for video editing, graphics work, 3D applications and gaming. Max chips are designed for professional graphics, high-resolution video and demanding 3D workflows, while Ultra provides Apple’s highest GPU performance. The M5 Max offers up to 40 GPU cores, while the M5 Ultra doubles that to 80 GPU cores. Both also have Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to speed up AI workloads.

RAM: Apple calls RAM Unified Memory. The MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB, which is probably the biggest drawback of that machine. Most Macs start with at least 16GB, which is plenty for everyday use, although we recommend choosing more if your budget allows because the memory cannot be upgraded later. 24GB or 32GB is a good choice for heavier multitasking, photo editing, podcasting, moderate video production and gaming. Developers and professional creative users may benefit from 48GB, 64GB or more. The new M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 64GB, M5 Max Mac Studio with up to 128GB, and M5 Ultra Mac Studio with an enormous 512GB.

Storage: Even with iCloud and external drives available, it can seem like you can never have enough storage inside your Mac. 256GB may be sufficient for basic web and office use, but it can fill up quickly. We recommend 512GB for most people who want to keep a Mac for several years, particularly if you store photos, games or media locally. For regular video or audio production, 1TB or more is preferable. Professional users may need several terabytes. The M5 Pro Mac mini offers up to 8TB, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio and touchscreen M5 Max MacBook Pro offer up to 16TB. Maximum capacity varies by model and chip, so check the configuration you’re considering. Choose enough internal storage when ordering rather than relying on a later internal upgrade. An external SSD can add capacity for media libraries, project files and archives, often at a lower cost than Apple’s internal storage upgrades.

Display: Consider screen quality and workspace alongside processing power. The MacBook Air’s display is suitable for everyday work and many creative tasks, while MacBook Pro models add XDR brightness and ProMotion refresh rates. What is it? The iMac is Apple’s all-in-one desktop, combining a computer and 24-inch display with a camera, speakers, keyboard and mouse. Its slim enclosure and seven color options make it an attractive choice for a home office, shared family workspace or business reception.

What’s new? Apple announced the M6 iMac on October 27, 2026, replacing the M4 generation and skipping M5. The main changes are additional CPU and GPU cores, improved AI processing, faster storage and upgraded connectivity, including Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and available 2.5Gb Ethernet. The design, colors, display and camera remain unchanged.

Who’s it for? The iMac suits families, students, home workers and small businesses that want a complete desktop setup with minimal clutter. It should also handle photo editing and other creative work, although demanding professional workloads may justify a Mac mini with M5 Pro or a Mac Studio. Those models also let you choose a larger display.

How much does the iMac cost? The two-port M6 iMac starts at $1,499/£1,499, while the four-port version starts at $1,699/£1,699. Both include 16GB of unified memory and a 256GB SSD. These starting prices match the outgoing M4 models following Apple’s June 2026 price increases.

What are the specifications? There are two main hardware versions, with different processors, connections and upgrade limits:

  • Two-port iMac: M6 with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, 16GB memory and a 256GB SSD, from $1,499/£1,499. Configurable with 24GB memory and up to 1TB storage.
  • Four-port iMac: M6 with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, 16GB memory and a 256GB SSD, from $1,699/£1,699. Configurable with 24GB or 32GB memory and up to 2TB storage.
  • Both include a dual 16-core Neural Engine and GPU Neural Accelerators.

What are the display specifications? Both versions retain the 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, measuring 23.5 inches diagonally. It has a resolution of 4,480 × 2,520, 500 nits of brightness, P3 wide color, support for a billion colors and True Tone. Nano-texture glass is an extra-cost option on the four-port model to reduce reflections.

How do I connect stuff? The entry-level iMac has two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports; the higher model has four. Both include a headphone jack, but USB-A accessories require an adapter or a suitable hub or dock. Wireless connectivity improves to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, replacing Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 on the previous generation. The four-port model includes 2.5Gb Ethernet, while it is an optional upgrade on the two-port version. You’ll need compatible network equipment to benefit from the faster Ethernet connection. The two-port model supports one external display, while the four-port version supports up to two, alongside the built-in screen.

How fast is it?: Apple claims up to 1.5 times faster performance in productivity tasks such as Excel, twice the graphics performance in selected workloads, and five times faster local AI prompt processing than M4. These figures describe Apple’s specified tests, rather than universal improvements across every app. Independent testing is needed to establish real-world gains and sustained performance. The four-port model’s additional CPU and GPU cores give it more processing resources than the entry-level version.

Any other considerations? The base 256GB SSD is restrictive if you keep large photo libraries, videos or games locally. Consider 512GB or more, or budget for an external SSD. Memory cannot be upgraded later, so choose enough for your likely longer-term needs. Compare the complete setup cost with a Mac mini plus a suitable display and accessories. The iMac’s integrated design is convenient, but a separate computer and monitor offer more flexibility when upgrading.

Why we recommend the iMac (M6): It’s a straightforward way to buy a complete Mac desktop with a sharp display, camera, good speakers and matching accessories. For buyers who need its additional features, the $1,699/£1,699 four-port model is worth the extra $200/£200: it adds more CPU and GPU cores, two additional ports, a Touch ID keyboard and included Ethernet, plus higher memory and storage limits. The two-port version remains sufficient for lighter everyday use.

FAQ

1.

What’s best, MacBook Air or MacBook Pro?

We explore this question in detail in our MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro comparison. The MacBook Air is the best choice for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work, studying and many creative tasks. The MacBook Pro is worth considering if you need sustained performance for demanding workloads, more ports or a more advanced display.

The entry-level MacBook Air costs $1,299/£1,299, although you can often spend less by shopping around – we regularly round up the best MacBook Air deals. If you want more screen space without paying for professional-level performance, the 15-inch MacBook Air is considerably cheaper than a 14-inch MacBook Pro.

Within the MacBook Pro range, the standard 14-inch M6 model provides a middle ground between the Air and the more expensive M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations. Its fan helps maintain performance during longer processing tasks, while its Liquid Retina XDR display, HDMI port and SDXC card slot add flexibility.

The M5 Pro and M5 Max models suit more demanding professional workloads, offering more CPU and GPU cores, higher memory capacities and Thunderbolt 5. M5 Pro is a strong option for software development, photography and video editing. Consider M5 Max if your work benefits from its additional graphics power, media engines or higher memory ceiling; spending more won’t necessarily make everyday tasks noticeably faster.

You can also choose a MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR touchscreen. Available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, these models add an OLED display, touch controls alongside the keyboard and trackpad, Dynamic Island, and a thinner, lighter design. Starting at $2,899/£2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399/£3,399 for the 16-inch, they cost $400/£400 more than equivalent non-touch M5 Pro models. They use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip families, so the main reasons to pay extra are the display, portability and touch input.

Choosing between a 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro comes down to workspace, portability, battery life and price. The larger model gives you more room for editing timelines, coding and multitasking, while the 14-inch is easier to carry. Both sizes offer powerful Pro and Max configurations. For external monitors, current M5 Pro models support up to three displays and M5 Max models support up to four, depending on resolution and refresh rate.

For a tighter budget, the MacBook Neo lowers the starting price of a Mac laptop to $699/£699. It’s worth comparing its compromises with a discounted previous-generation MacBook Air before deciding.

2.

Should I upgrade from my Intel Mac?

Yes. It’s time! We are now more than six years into Apple’s transition from Intel processors to its own silicon that includes CPU, GPU, and unified memory. The transition began with the introduction of the M1 in November 2020. Since June 2023 every Mac Apple sells uses Apple’s own chips rather than Intel processors.

If you’ve yet to upgrade your Intel Mac to one powered by Apple’s silicon what are you waiting for? If you are concerned that a must-have app doesn’t run on an M-series Mac, consider finding a new app because the performance gains are tremendous.

Another good reason to replace an Intel Mac is that Apple’s support for these models is winding down. macOS Golden Gate, released in September 2026, is the first major version of macOS to support no Intel Macs. Intel Macs compatible with older versions of macOS may continue receiving security updates for a limited period, but they are now outside Apple’s current feature-release cycle. Apple does not guarantee how long those updates will continue, and machines limited to macOS Sequoia are likely to lose support sooner than those capable of running macOS Tahoe. Read: How long does Apple support Macs.

4.

What specs do I really need for my Mac?

Chip: The specs you need depend on what you plan to do with your Mac. For web browsing, email, office apps and light photo editing, a standard M-series chip is more than sufficient. The M6 is available in the Mac mini, iMac and standard 14-inch MacBook Pro, while the MacBook Air uses M5. The budget MacBook Neo uses an A18 Pro chip. A newer generation number doesn’t automatically make a chip better for every workload: compare its CPU, GPU, memory and capabilities with what your apps actually need.

If you regularly work with complex spreadsheets, large Photoshop files, audio projects, video editing or more demanding games, look at a Pro chip. The M5 Pro Mac mini, for example, offers up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU and up to 64GB unified memory.

A Max chip is worth considering for demanding graphics, complex 3D work, high-resolution video production or projects that need more memory than a Pro configuration supports. Many developers, photographers and video editors will be well served by a Pro chip. The M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and up to 128GB unified memory, depending on configuration.

For professional video production, 3D work, software development and other intensive workloads, a Max chip is more appropriate. The Mac Studio with M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and as much as 128GB unified memory. 

The M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU and 512GB unified memory, is aimed at the most extreme workloads, including VFX, scientific computing and running very large AI models locally.

GPU: One of the biggest differences between Apple’s chips is GPU performance. Standard M-series chips are easily sufficient for everyday graphics, casual gaming and light creative work. Pro chips add considerably more GPU power for video editing, graphics work, 3D applications and gaming. Max chips are designed for professional graphics, high-resolution video and demanding 3D workflows, while Ultra provides Apple’s highest GPU performance. The M5 Max offers up to 40 GPU cores, while the M5 Ultra doubles that to 80 GPU cores. Both also have Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to speed up AI workloads.

RAM: Apple calls RAM Unified Memory. The MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB, which is probably the biggest drawback of that machine. Most Macs start with at least 16GB, which is plenty for everyday use, although we recommend choosing more if your budget allows because the memory cannot be upgraded later. 24GB or 32GB is a good choice for heavier multitasking, photo editing, podcasting, moderate video production and gaming. Developers and professional creative users may benefit from 48GB, 64GB or more. The new M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 64GB, M5 Max Mac Studio with up to 128GB, and M5 Ultra Mac Studio with an enormous 512GB.

Storage: Even with iCloud and external drives available, it can seem like you can never have enough storage inside your Mac. 256GB may be sufficient for basic web and office use, but it can fill up quickly. We recommend 512GB for most people who want to keep a Mac for several years, particularly if you store photos, games or media locally. For regular video or audio production, 1TB or more is preferable. Professional users may need several terabytes. The M5 Pro Mac mini offers up to 8TB, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio and touchscreen M5 Max MacBook Pro offer up to 16TB. Maximum capacity varies by model and chip, so check the configuration you’re considering. Choose enough internal storage when ordering rather than relying on a later internal upgrade. An external SSD can add capacity for media libraries, project files and archives, often at a lower cost than Apple’s internal storage upgrades.

Display: Consider screen quality and workspace alongside processing power. The MacBook Air’s display is suitable for everyday work and many creative tasks, while MacBook Pro models add XDR brightness and ProMotion refresh rates. The PROLED XDR models also offer OLED, Adobe RGB support and touchscreen input in a lighter design. Choose them if those features will benefit how you work; they use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip families as the non-touch versions.

For more information to help you decide which Mac to buy see our Mac processor comparison where we compare Apple silicon and Intel. We also offer advice about how much storage, RAM, and cores in How much MacBook RAM, SSD, GPU, and CPU do you really need.

Apple discontinued the Mac Pro in March 2026. The Mac Studio is now its highest-end desktop Mac.

Apple rarely arrives first to the party, but it tends to deliver an innovative twist when it eventually catches up to its rivals. AirPods, Face ID, Apple Watch, even the iPhone Duo weren’t the first of their kind, but they stood out for their leaps in design and functionality. However, as the launch of Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro just proved, that’s not always the case.

Commercial touchscreen laptops have been around for almost two decades. Despite that, standard models have remained the default for valid reasons, most notably due to their perfect ergonomics. Instead of perfecting the formula as it usually does, Apple distracted fans with a recycled favorite—slapping on a glowing logo that had been retired a decade ago.

What makes the touchscreen MacBook especially baffling is how unnecessary it is. Apple already figured out the touchscreen setup back in 2019, and it’s been hiding in plain sight all these years.

Sidecar attachment

Sidecar was released as part of macOS Catalina in 2019. Billed as a way to expand your workspace, it essentially lets you use an iPad as an external wireless display for your Mac. Once it’s connected via AirPlay, you can drag Mac windows to your iPad’s screen and interact with them as you would on your Mac. Most controls were previously limited to Apple Pencil or mouse and keyboard input, but with macOS 27, you can use your fingers, too. There’s even a handy Sidebar on the ‌iPad‌ for common controls, like bringing up the on-screen keyboard or returning to the iPad’s Home screen, along with the Touch Bar that was previously included with certain MacBook models.

Apple

Unhinged design

Steve Jobs famously opposed touchscreen laptops because “after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off.” When reading early rumors about the touchscreen MacBook, I had expected—or at least hoped—Apple would do something different by incorporating an innovative hinge mechanism. A convertible form factor would have allowed users to interact with the touchscreen horizontally and easily switch back to the traditional laptop mode whenever needed. Alas, that did not come to fruition.

I acknowledge that we shouldn’t take everything Steve ever said as gospel because technology evolves, but many of his remarks still hold true today. The main issue with touchscreen laptops has never been weight or thickness, as some Apple execs recently suggested. At no point while using my MacBook does it feel natural for me to extend my arm and touch its display, and most people would probably relate. The new MacBook Pro is no different, and a sturdier hinge and lighter chassis don’t resolve the actual problem.

Sidecar is a whole different story, however. My iPad is untethered from the MacBook’s keyboard, letting me flexibly touch its screen horizontally or otherwise. This allows me to utilize touch input on macOS when the need arises without straining my arm. It’s precisely the kind of innovation Apple is generally praised for, and we’ve already had it for years.

Out of touch

The MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR Display caters to professional creatives by letting them interact with macOS apps using their fingers. Yet, curiously, the machine is seemingly incompatible with many of these professional creatives’ go-to accessory: the Apple Pencil. This bars power users from taking advantage of precise interactions, pressure sensitivity, tilt detection, and all the other perks they cannot achieve with their fingers.

Meanwhile, Sidecar on the iPad supports Apple Pencil input—not to mention that iPadOS can run many desktop-class creative suites natively. So, whether you’re Sidecar-ing or using the iPad independently, you get to unlock advanced creation controls and workflows that surpass what you can do with the new MacBook Pro.

Beyond functionality, using an Apple Pencil minimizes fingerprints on your display, and creators know all too well how relevant that is. I’m far from being a professional photographer, but I’m constantly wiping down my 13-inch iPad Pro M4 before editing pictures because color correction and healing blemishes on the pixel level require that kind of clarity. Without Apple Pencil support, the new MacBook Pro’s display is going to get all smudgy as you attempt to get work done.

Apple

Mac Duo

Another advantage for using Sidecar as a separate wireless monitor for your Mac is having two sets of app windows open on each screen simultaneously to work on more complex tasks. Touch Bar enthusiasts will also be delighted to learn that the discontinued MacBook feature lives on through Sidecar.

Non-MacBook Pro users, like those with a Mac mini/Studio, MacBook Air, or iMac, will especially appreciate being able to utilize the touchscreen without spending almost $3,000 on a new laptop—all thanks to Sidecar. In fact, it might be wiser to buy a Mac mini and an iPad Pro than a touchscreen MacBook Pro. Let’s break it down.

An M5 Pro Mac mini ($1,699) combined with an iPad Pro M5 ($1,199) costs $2,898—a dollar less than the touchscreen MacBook Pro (M5 Pro)’s starting price. With this package, you’d be getting one of the most advanced tandem OLED panels on the market and two desktop-grade processors instead of one, not to mention Apple Pencil support and far greater versatility.

Foundry

Pick a side

I’ve long depended on Sidecar with my MacBook Air, and—unlike the touchscreen MacBook Pro—it remains a prominent example of Apple’s classic “It just works” philosophy. The built-in feature requires absolutely no setup, cables, or technical literacy. Your Mac magically pairs to your nearby iPad and lets you mirror or extend the display wirelessly. That’s the epitome of touchscreen support on a laptop, even surpassing the highly advanced convertibles in terms of practicality and overall user experience.

Ultimately, if touchscreen laptops were truly essential, they would’ve evolved meaningfully throughout the past years, and Apple wouldn’t have waited this long to release one. Professionals have been using standard laptops for decades just fine, and add-ons like Wacom graphics tablets continue to thrive among digital artists due to their precision and horizontal designs.

Steve Jobs once said that people don’t know what they want until you show it to them. Apple already showed us the right way to do touch on a Mac with Sidecar, and it shouldn’t have caved to market pressure to build the wrong one.

Apple’s “Pro and Tell” media experience, took place in Los Angeles on October 28, 2026. The company announced its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, officially called MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, featuring tandem OLED, Dynamic Island and a thinner, lighter design.

It completed a week of announcements that included the iPad mini with A20 Pro on October 26 and the standard 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro and M6 iMac on October 27. Preorders are open, with availability beginning November 6.

Apple has not announced a date for its next event. Attention now turns to possible spring 2027 launches, although new products could arrive through press releases or another media experience rather than a keynote.

Apple’s annual event calendar typically includes WWDC in June and the iPhone event in September, with additional launches sometimes taking place in spring and October. Dates are rarely confirmed far in advance, but past schedules and reliable reporting offer clues for anyone planning to buy a new Apple device. Here’s everything we know about Apple’s next event, including the date, start time, expected announcements and what could follow.

When is Apple’s next event?

Spring 2027 is the next likely window for an Apple event, although the company has not confirmed a date.

Over the past decade, Apple has held spring events and media experiences on several dates:

  • March 4, 2026
  • May 7, 2024
  • March 8, 2022
  • April 20, 2021
  • March 25, 2019
  • March 27, 2018

Apple can also announce products without holding an event. In 2025, it introduced the iPhone 16e in February, followed in March by the seventh-generation iPad Air, 11th-generation iPad, MacBook Air and Mac Studio.

That makes spring 2027 a plausible window for further launches, whether Apple holds an event, invites the media to a hands-on experience or announces products through press releases.

Is it really all that 'Modern'?

Just in case the news passed you by, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launched on Switch 2 this month — the first in the series to do so since the Wii U days. Naturally, a lot of the attention has been on the game's performance and whether the Switch 2 would be able to keep up with its competitors. Here to answer exactly that are the tech experts over at Digital Foundry, who have just shared their thoughts on the hybrid version's nitty-gritty details.

We'll start with the all-important frame rates. DF states that MW4 runs at 30fps in its campaign mode, 60fps in competitive multiplayer, and 40fps (if you have a 120Hz display hooked up) in the DMZ extraction mode. While this is a little lower than other platforms — particularly in the campaign respect — it does mean that we Switch 2 players can still get the full-fat CoD experience.
